findings.title: Google Meet fallback crashes when booking has no destination calendar
findings.body: In `create()`, the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then evaluates `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` when `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. When the event has no destination calendar (`null` from handleNewBooking, or `[]` from confirm/payment flows), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws a TypeError. This is exactly the scenario this branch exists for ("Fallback to Cal Video if Google Meet is selected w/o a Google Cal"), so any booking with a Google Meet location and no destination calendar now crashes instead of falling back to Daily. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`); this needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

findings.title: IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition for org slug is inverted
findings.body: This PR (which is about destination calendars) changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the condition. Previously, when team billing was disabled (e.g. self-hosted), the org got its `slug` immediately, and when billing was enabled only `requestedSlug` was stored so the real slug could be set after payment. After this change, billing-enabled installs set `slug` before payment (bypassing the paid flow) and billing-disabled installs never set a slug at all, leaving the organization without a usable URL. This looks like an accidental flip during an unrelated edit and should be reverted.

findings.title: updateEvent fallback for missing externalCalendarId is dead code; updates fail with calendarId undefined
findings.body: In `updateEvent`, the new fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. That `.find` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares each calendar's `externalId` against `null`/`""` and can never match — `selectedCalendar` is always `undefined` in that case, and `calendar.events.update` is then called with `calendarId: undefined`, which throws and leaves the Google event un-updated (caught upstream as success=false, so the booking is rescheduled in cal.com but the calendar event keeps the old time). The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. This matters more now because other changes in this PR create references with `externalCalendarId: null` (see EventManager updateLocation and the no-credentialId create branch). The same dead `.find` pattern exists in `deleteEvent` (line 315-317), where it is only masked by the later `calendarId ? calendarId : "primary"` fallback.

findings.title: Video booking references lose credentialId, breaking meeting deletion on cancel
findings.body: In `create()`'s `referencesToCreate`, the credentialId is now `isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Previously it was `isCalendarType ? evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId : result.credentialId`, i.e. video results kept `result.credentialId` from `createMeeting`. With this change, every newly created video BookingReference is stored with `credentialId: null`. `handleCancelBooking` only deletes the video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set (it looks up the credential by id to call `deleteMeeting`), so cancelling bookings created after this change will leave orphaned Zoom/Daily/etc. meetings that are never deleted. There is no reason to special-case calendar types here; use `result.credentialId` for all results.

findings.title: updateLocation references are created without credentialId/externalCalendarId
findings.body: `updateLocation()` now builds references with `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined`, but the calendar-update results come from `updateAllCalendarEvents` → `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, whose returned EventResult never sets `externalId` or `credentialId`. Both fields are therefore always `undefined`, and `editLocation.handler` persists these references on the booking (`references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`). The old code fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` / `?.credentialId`. Consequence: bookings that go through "edit location" accumulate calendar references with no credential/calendar linkage, so later updates/deletes can't find the right credential and fall into legacy paths (including the broken Google `updateEvent` fallback).

findings.title: Office365 createEvent always targets the main host's calendar, even when creating for another host
findings.body: `createEvent` now takes the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (`mainHostDestinationCalendar`) and posts to `/me/calendars/{mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId}/events`. For collective events, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` calls `createEvent` once per host with that host's credential, but the full event (with all destination calendars, main host first) is passed each time. So when creating the event for a non-organizer host's Office365 account, it tries to write to the main host's calendar id using the team member's token, which fails (404/403) — the team member never gets the event. `CalendarManager.createEvent` already receives the per-destination `externalId` but doesn't forward it to `calendar.createEvent`; the credentialId-based lookup used in the Google service (or forwarding externalId) is needed here too.

findings.title: Lark createEvent uses the first destination calendar regardless of which host's credential is used
findings.body: Same class of bug as the Office365 service: `createEvent` derives `calendarId` from `event.destinationCalendar[0]` (the main host's calendar). For collective bookings, EventManager invokes `createEvent` separately for each host's credential, but Lark will always attempt `POST /calendar/v4/calendars/{mainHostCalendarId}/events/create_event` with the team member's token, which the member has no access to — so non-organizer hosts never get Lark calendar events. The service should select the destination calendar matching the credential being used (as the Google service now does with the credentialId parameter).

findings.title: CalDAV createEvent silently reports success without creating anything for other hosts
findings.body: The CalDAV base service filters `calendars` to `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. When EventManager creates the event for a non-organizer host's CalDAV credential (collective events), that host's account does not contain the main host's calendar URL, so the filtered list is empty, `Promise.all([])` resolves to `[]`, `responses.some(r => !r.ok)` is false, and the method returns a successful result with a uid — but no event was created anywhere. This is a silent data-integrity failure: the booking reference is stored, but the team member's calendar has no event. It should match the destination calendar for the credential in use, like Google's credentialId lookup.

findings.title: Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer and event type have none
findings.body: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and the collective-team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Optional chaining means that when the base value is `null`, the push is silently skipped: for a collective event where the organizer has no connected destination calendar but team members do, none of the team members' calendars receive events (and the booking's destinationCalendar is not connected either). The array should be initialized to `[]` (or the team calendars assigned directly) so collective hosts still get their events.

findings.title: Dynamic user query no longer selects organization
findings.body: The `loadUsers` refactor rewrote the dynamic-group user lookup and dropped `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select (it was explicitly selected before, together with `metadata`). Any downstream code for dynamic collective bookings that reads `user.organization.slug` (e.g. org-subdomain/booker-url handling) will now get `undefined` and potentially throw. This removal is unrelated to the destination-calendar change and looks accidental; it should be restored.

findings.title: Recurring-event deletion block now runs once per calendar reference
findings.body: The recurring-cancellation branch (mapping over all of the organizer's calendar credentials × all updated recurring bookings and deleting each) lives inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With multiple calendar references (the collective multi-host case this PR introduces, typically one per host), the entire recurring deletion pass executes once per reference, issuing duplicate `deleteEvent` calls for the same events. Google tolerates this via 404/410 handling, but other providers may log errors and it doubles the external API traffic. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop. (Separately, that branch still only deletes the first calendar reference per updated booking, so team-member calendar events for recurring collective bookings remain stale.)

findings.title: Hangout-link patch call uses possibly-undefined calendarId
findings.body: In `createEvent`, the insert call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (that writes the description with the hangout link) passes the raw `selectedCalendar`, which is `undefined` whenever no destination calendar matches the credentialId. The google client will throw a missing-parameter error for that patch, so the hangout link is never written into the event description in that case. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always defined (defaulted to "primary").

findings.title: Only the first old calendar event is deleted when merging bookings on reschedule
findings.body: When `newBookingId` is set (reschedule/merge path), the code deletes the old booking's calendar event via `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))`. Bookings can now have multiple calendar references (one per collective host), so only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep a stale event at the old time. This should iterate over all calendar references of the old booking.

findings.title: Webhook payload sends destinationCalendar as null in some flows and [] in others
findings.body: The updated e2e expectations now encode that BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED payloads contain `destinationCalendar: null` while BOOKING_REJECTED contains `destinationCalendar: []` — because handleNewBooking emits `null` when there is no destination calendar while confirm.handler emits `[]`. This is an inconsistent contract for the same field across webhook triggers, and the field's shape also changed from a single object to an array, which is a breaking change for existing webhook consumers despite the PR being labelled non-breaking. Consider normalizing (always array, or always null-when-empty) across all emitters.

findings.title: No automated tests cover the new multi-destination calendar logic
findings.body: The PR rewrites `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` and the create/update/delete paths of four calendar providers for the collective multi-host scenario, but the author explicitly checked "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". The only test change is a webhook payload expectation. Regressions introduced here (e.g. the Google Meet fallback TypeError, non-Google providers writing to the main host's calendar, video references losing credentialId) would be caught by even a minimal unit test around `EventManager.create` with multiple destination calendars.
